title: Maximum Number of Groups Getting Fresh Donuts
statement:
A donut shop bakes in batches of exactly `batchSize` donuts and only starts a new batch once every donut of the current one has been handed out. Each `groups[i]` is the size of one group of customers. Every customer receives one donut, and a group is served completely before the next group begins.

A group is **happy** when its first customer gets a donut from a freshly started batch, that is, when the number of donuts handed out before that group is a multiple of `batchSize` (so whichever group is served first is always happy). You may serve the groups in any order. Return the largest possible number of happy groups.
notes:
## Intuition

A group is happy exactly when the donuts served before it add up to a multiple of `batchSize`, so only each size **modulo** `batchSize` matters. Trying all orders (the brute force) is hopeless for 30 groups.

Two kinds of groups can be settled up front. A group with remainder 0 always leaves the batch boundary where it found it, so serving all of them first makes every one happy. Starting on a batch boundary, a group with remainder `r` followed by one with remainder `batchSize - r` ends on a boundary again, so each such pair yields one happy group; pairing them off greedily never loses, because any arrangement can be reshuffled to put a complementary pair in a block of its own.

What is left is a memoized search. The future depends only on **how many groups of each remainder remain**; even the current leftover is fixed by that (it is the served total mod `batchSize`). After pairing, at most one side of each pair survives, so there are only a few thousand states.

## Approach

1. Count the groups by remainder in `count`; every remainder-0 group adds to `happy`.
2. For each `r` with `r <= other = batchSize - r`, remove `pairs` matched groups (two of the same remainder when `r === other`) and add `pairs` to `happy`.
3. `best(leftover)` returns the most happy groups among those still waiting, with `leftover` donuts of the current batch already used. The next group is happy only if `leftover === 0`, worth `gain = 1`.
4. Try each `r` with `count[r] > 0`: serve one such group, recurse with `(leftover + r) % batchSize`, then undo.
5. Memoize on `count.join(',')` and return `happy + best(0)`.

## Example 1, step by step

`batchSize = 3`, `groups = [1,2,3,4,5,6]` have remainders `[1,2,0,1,2,0]`, so `count = [2,2,2]` and `happy = 2` (sizes 3 and 6). For `r = 1`, `other = 2`: `pairs = min(2, 2) = 2`, so `happy = 4` and `count = [0,0,0]`. Nothing is left for the search, `best(0) = 0`, and the answer is **4**, e.g. order `[3,6,1,2,4,5]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(S · batchSize²), where S = ∏(count[r] + 1) after pairing; with at most four surviving remainders and 30 groups, S stays around 5,000.
- Space: O(S) for the memo, plus recursion depth up to `groups.length`.

## Pitfalls

- When `batchSize` is even, remainder `batchSize / 2` pairs with itself: take `floor(count / 2)` pairs.
- With no group left, `best` must return 0, not `gain`: the bonus belongs to a group actually served.
- Work with `size % batchSize`; never store raw totals (up to 3·10^10) in the state.
- Skipping the pairing step leaves up to about 250,000 states, which is slow in an interpreter.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count[r]` | groups still waiting whose size has remainder `r` |
| `happy` | happy groups settled before the search |
| `other`, `pairs` | the complementary remainder and how many pairs were matched |
| `leftover` | donuts of the current batch already handed out |
| `gain` | 1 if the next group served is happy, else 0 |
| `memo` | best result for each `count` state |
| `result` | best total over all choices of the next group |
